Manage
The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.

criteria.title: Incident documentation
criteria.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
criteria.reasoning: No explicit minimum information set or root cause/missing-information handling is present; the retrieved text only references general incident tracking, post-deployment monitoring, and incident response, which do not satisfy the EU-specified indicators. Alignment_overreach confirms reliance on generic processes rather than the required minimum data elements.
key_aligned_concepts: Incident tracking and documentation
Post-deployment monitoring and incident response
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing defined categories of information to document for serious incidents (e.g., timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
No explicit requirement for root cause analysis including examination of model outputs/inputs and failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
Lack of guidance on how post-market monitoring signals inform incident analysis.
No explicit handling of missing information (recording information gaps at reporting time).
No proportionality guidance tying detail level to incident severity.
No explicit external/regulatory reporting obligations or timelines beyond internal tracking (if applicable).
Alignment_overreach: Existing MANAGE 4, MANAGE 4.1, and MANAGE 4.3 language describes processes and monitoring but does not implement the required minimum information set.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The retrieved AI RMF 1.0 text does not specify a minimum information set for serious incident documentation or root cause analysis or handling of missing information; it only notes that incidents and errors are tracked, communicated to relevant actors, and that post-deployment monitoring and incident response processes exist and are documented.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text acknowledges incident tracking and documentation, and post-deployment monitoring, but it does not provide the required minimum information categories or explicit root cause analysis and missing information handling as per the EU requirement.
key_aligned_concepts: Incident tracking and documentation
Post-deployment monitoring and incident response

evidence_citations.quote: MANAGE 4.3: Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities. Processes for tracking, responding to, and recovering from incidents and errors are followed and documented.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows operational handling of incidents but not the minimum information set.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Not explicitly addressed by the indicators.

evidence_citations.quote: MANAGE 4: Risk treatments, including response and recovery, and communication plans for the identified and measured AI risks are documented and monitored regularly.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that incidents and responses are planned and documented at a high level, not the required information set.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Not explicitly addressed by the indicators.

evidence_citations.quote: MANAGE 4.1: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Indicates existence of monitoring and incident response processes but does not define minimum data elements for serious incident reports.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Not explicitly addressed by the indicators.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The AI RMF 1.0 does not specify a minimum information set or explicit root-cause analysis requirements for serious incidents, nor does it provide handling for missing information, explicit patterns from post-market monitoring informing incident analysis, or proportionality of detail to incident severity. It only references general incident tracking and post-deployment monitoring without the EU-required specifics.
missing_elements: Defined categories of information to document for serious incidents (e.g., timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
Explicit requirement for root cause analysis including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
Clear guidance on how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring inform incident analysis.
Explicit handling of missing information (e.g., procedures for explicitly recording information gaps at the time of reporting).
Proportionality guidance tying the level of detail in incident documentation to the severity of the incident.
Explicit external/regulatory reporting obligations or timelines (if applicable) beyond internal tracking.
weaker_areas: Post-deployment monitoring exists (MANAGE 4.1) but there is no explicit linkage to incident analysis data elements or minimum data categories for serious incidents.
Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors and affected communities (MANAGE 4.3), but this lacks predefined data categories, templates, or severity-based detail requirements.
scope_divergences: Divergence from EU requirements by focusing on internal incident management language (tracking, responding, recovering, and communicating to actors) rather than specifying the minimum information set to track, document, and report for serious incidents, including root-cause analysis and handling of incomplete information.
Lack of explicit guidance on how post-market monitoring signals should inform incident analysis and how the level of detail should scale with incident severity.
alignment_overreach: MANAGE 4: Risk treatments, including response and recovery, and communication plans for the identified and measured AI risks are documented and monitored regularly, which does not equate to the EU-required minimum information categories or root-cause/reporting specifics.

MANAGE 4.1: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including capturing/evaluating input from users and AI actors, appeal/override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management—this describes processes but not a defined information set for serious incident documentation.

MANAGE 4.3: Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities, with processes for tracking/responding/recovering—this addresses communication but not the explicit data elements or external reporting obligations required by the EU.

synthesis_result.justification: No explicit minimum information set or root cause/missing-information handling is present; the retrieved text only references general incident tracking, post-deployment monitoring, and incident response, which do not satisfy the EU-specified indicators. Alignment_overreach confirms reliance on generic processes rather than the required minimum data elements.

No explicit requirement for root cause analysis including examination of model outputs/inputs and failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
Lack of guidance on how post-market monitoring signals inform incident analysis.
No explicit handling of missing information (recording information gaps at reporting time).
No proportionality guidance tying detail level to incident severity.
No explicit external/regulatory reporting obligations or timelines beyond internal tracking (if applicable).
Alignment_overreach: Existing MANAGE 4, MANAGE 4.1, and MANAGE 4.3 language describes processes and monitoring but does not implement the required minimum information set.

criteria.title: Reporting timelines
criteria.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
The framework allows aggregation of multiple similar serious incidents within defined reporting timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.
criteria.reasoning: No indicators of severity-based, time-bound incident reporting are present. The text only references general reporting/documentation requirements without operational timelines, triggers, cadences, or final-resolution reporting. Missing elements include incident categories, severity-differentiated initial deadlines, awareness-based reporting trigger, periodic updates, final resolution deadline, and aggregation rules; these unmet indicators cannot be offset by thematic alignment.

Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and

Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The
first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will
change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number
(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time
and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

practices, methodologies, and tools for managing AI risks – as well as illustrate the
need for additional, improved resources.

abilities to operate under applicable domestic and international legal or regulatory
regimes.
10. Be a living document. The AI RMF should be readily updated as technology, understanding, and approaches to AI trustworthiness and uses of AI change and as stakeholders learn from implementing AI risk management generally and this framework
in particular.
